blurb: Anxiety is persistent worry, tension, or fear that interferes with daily life. Substances used 'for anxiety' act on GABA-A (benzodiazepines, barbiturates, alcohol, GHB), on serotonin reuptake (SSRIs/SNRIs), on histamine/orexin (sedating antihistamines), or on alpha-2-delta (gabapentinoids). Non-addictive first-line options include SSRIs/SNRIs/buspirone; GABAergic options carry dependence and overdose risk, especially combined with opioids or alcohol.

Depression is persistent low mood, loss of interest, and low energy for two or more weeks. It is treated with antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, MAOIs, bupropion, mirtazapine, esketamine). MAOIs carry serotonin syndrome risk with stimulants, empathogens and SSRIs; mind the washout rules.

Pain is divided into nociceptive (tissue damage), inflammatory, and neuropathic (nerve damage). Opioids and NSAIDs cover nociceptive and inflammatory pain; neuropathic pain responds better to gabapentinoids, TCAs, SNRIs. Dual mu-agonist + NRI agents (tapentadol, tramadol) hit both.

ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition of impaired attention and impulse control. It is treated with stimulants (amphetamine, methylphenidate) or wakefulness agents that boost dopamine and norepinephrine. Tachyphylaxis develops within-session and tolerance builds over months.

Insomnia is persistent difficulty falling or staying asleep despite opportunity. Sedatives help short-term: Z-drugs, benzodiazepines, orexin antagonists, trazodone, mirtazapine, melatonin, sedating antihistamines. Long-term GABAergic sedative use leads to tolerance and rebound insomnia.

Epilepsy is a tendency to recurrent seizures. Anticonvulsants (valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, benzodiazepines, phenobarbital) raise seizure threshold via sodium-channel blockade, GABA enhancement, or SV2A binding.
High blood pressure is treated with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium-channel blockers, diuretics, and beta-blockers. Stimulants, cocaine and nicotine raise BP; alpha-2 agonists (clonidine) lower it.

Diabetes is impaired glucose regulation. Type 1 is autoimmune; Type 2 is insulin resistance. Treatments include insulin, metformin, GLP-1 agonists and sulfonylureas. Alcohol causes delayed hypoglycemia; stimulants can affect glucose control.

Asthma is reversible airway narrowing with inflammation. Relievers are beta-2 agonists (albuterol); controllers are inhaled corticosteroids, LABAs, leukotriene antagonists, anticholinergics. Beta-blockers are contraindicated because they cause bronchospasm.

The cough reflex is mediated by airway irritation. Suppressants: dextromethorphan (NMDA/sigma-1), codeine (mu-opioid), benzonatate. Expectorants thin mucus. Note dextromethorphan's abuse potential as a dissociative.

Migraine is a neurovascular headache with cortical spreading depolarization. Acute: triptans (5-HT1B/1D), NSAIDs, CGRP antagonists. Preventive: beta-blockers, amitriptyline, valproate, topiramate, CGRP monoclonal antibodies.

Infections are treated with antimicrobials that inhibit essential microbial processes: cell wall synthesis (beta-lactams), protein synthesis (tetracyclines, macrolides), DNA replication (fluoroquinolones). Resistance is a major problem; completing prescribed courses matters.

Nausea involves the chemoreceptor trigger zone and vomiting center. Antiemetics: dopamine antagonists, 5-HT3 antagonists (ondansetron), antihistamines, muscarinic antagonists (scopolamine). Serotonin syndrome risk when 5-HT3 antagonists combine with MAOIs.

Allergic reactions involve histamine and immune mediators. Antihistamines block H1 (diphenhydramine and hydroxyzine sedate; loratadine and cetirizine less so). Severe anaphylaxis is treated with epinephrine and corticosteroids.
Staying asleep through the night. Interacts with alcohol's zero-order clearance and with benzodiazepine tolerance.
